cards.explanation: The answer is to keep discretion and knowledge. The father says it right in verse 2: “…that you may maintain discretion and your lips may preserve knowledge.” Close listening is how the son holds on to both. I think that's a great trade, friends. It's a lot like keeping a good recipe card out of the flour bin.

The answer is bitter. Verse 4 says, “…in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword.” Wormwood is a plant known for its bitter taste. The honey comes first and the bitter comes last, so the father wants his son to look at the end of the road. Verse 3 says her lips drip honey, friends, but that's only where it starts.

The answer is down to death. Verse 5 says, “Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol.” Sheol is the realm of the dead. Notice the word straight. The father isn't describing a scenic route, friends. He's describing a road that goes one way.

The answer is False. Verse 6 says, “She does not consider the path of life; she does not know that her ways are unstable.” So she does not consider the path of life at all, friends. The father adds that her ways are unstable, and she doesn't know it.
The answer is True. Verse 8 says, “Keep your path far from her…” The father follows it by telling his sons not to go near the door of her house. He means far, friends, not a casual stroll past.

The answer is True. Verse 9 warns, “…lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel…” Both his vigor and his years are at stake, friends, and the father doesn't want them handed over. That's why he says to keep far away in verse 8.

The answer is strangers. Verse 10 says, “…lest strangers feast on your wealth…” It goes on to say that his labors enrich the house of a foreigner. Imagine baking all week and a stranger walks off with the whole box, friends. That's the picture, and the father wants to spare his son from it.

The answer is that he hated correction and ignored his teachers. The son says, “How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!” and then, “I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors.” (Proverbs 5:12-13) That's a hard thing to say at the end of a life, friends. It's why the father begins the whole chapter by asking his son to listen.

The answer is False. In the father's warning, the groaning son says, “I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly.” It's not hidden at all, friends. It happens in the midst of the whole assembly, and it's a heavy line.

The answer is his own cistern and well. Verse 15 says, “Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” A cistern is a pit that holds water. The father says own twice, friends, so the water he points to is the son's.

The answer is wife. Verse 18 says, “May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth…” After talking about water, the father turns to the son's own wife, friends. He wants his son to find his joy at home.

The answer is, why be captivated by an adulteress. Verse 20 says, “Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?” The father has just wished his son joy with his own wife, friends. Now he asks why anyone would look elsewhere.

The answer is False. Verse 21 says, “For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths.” The word is all, friends, so none are left out. It's a steady thing to know.

The answer is his own sins. Verse 22 says, “The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him.” Iniquities means sins. The thing that holds him is his own, friends, and that's a sobering thought.

The answer is discipline. Verse 23 says, “He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly.” That word brings the whole chapter together, friends. Early on the father asked his son to listen, and the groaning man in verse 12 said he hated discipline.
